FCs: [0] S-1,C0,N0; [1] S0,C0,N-1; [2] S+1,C0,N-2. [0] and [1] tie on zeros; the tiebreak puts -1 on the more electronegative N (3.0 > 2.5), so [1]. (In reality S-C#N also contributes a lot; the textbook criteria pick [1].)
Formal charges pick the best of several nonequivalent valid Lewis structures.
The formal charges must add up to the overall charge (0 for a neutral molecule); +1+0+0 means there's an error.
3 + 3(7) = 24; the best structure has three B-F single bonds (all FC 0), leaving B with 6 electrons. A B=F double bond would put +1 on F.
7 + 2(6) = 19 is odd, so one electron is unpaired and ClO2 is a free radical.
Five P-F single bonds and no lone pair on P: 5 x 2 = 10 electrons (expanded octet).
42 valence e-: 10 in bonds + 30 on the F atoms leaves 2 (one lone pair) on Br, so Br has 10 + 2 = 12.
Only S (period 3) can expand its octet; N, C, and O are period 2.
The more electronegative O keeps its octet, and the odd electron stays on N (e.g., in NO, N=O gives FC 0 on both atoms).
Free radical = a species (atom, ion, or molecule) with one or more unpaired electrons.

26 e-. All single bonds: S = 6-2-3 = +1 and each O = -1. With one S=O: S 0, O= 0, two O -1; S has 2+2+4 bonding + 2 lone = 10. Two S=O would give S -1 (same count of zeros, negative on the less electronegative atom), so one double bond is best.
NO2 has 5 + 12 = 17 (odd); CO2 has 16, O3 18, NO3- 24.
N would have 6 (triple bond) + 2 (lone pair) + 1 = 9 electrons, which is more than a period-2 atom can hold. The total of 11 e- is correct.
In the N-N-O arrangement the two bonds differ, so the dipole changes during the symmetric stretch: IR-active.
A homonuclear H-H bond is nonpolar, so stretching it produces no changing dipole: IR-inactive.
The asymmetric stretch and the bend are IR-active; the symmetric stretch is inactive. (The bend is doubly degenerate, but the figure shows three vibrations.)
Wien's law: lambda_max = 2.898e-3/287 = about 10 um, which is infrared.
The excited CO2 re-emits an IR photon of about the same energy in a random direction, so it is as likely to go back toward Earth as out to space.
Bond vibrational frequencies fall in the IR range, and absorption requires the light's frequency to match.

The ends differ (C=O polar with a chi difference of 1.0; C=S nonpolar with 0), so no mode cancels: the symmetric stretch, asymmetric stretch, and bend all change the dipole. Real OCS shows all three IR bands.
CO is heteronuclear with a polar bond; N2, Cl2, and O2 are homonuclear and nonpolar.
Greenhouse activity requires IR absorption (a changing dipole), not abundance; the N2 and O2 bond stretches are IR-inactive.
